title: B1 Writing Quiz 5 — Work, Money & Ambitions

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I earned more money, I would save half of it.
If I earn more money, I would save half of it.
If I earned more money, I will save half of it.
If I would earn more money, I would save half of it.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I earned more money, I would save half of it.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she had accepted the job offer, she wouldn't move abroad.
If she had accepted the job offer, she wouldn't have moved abroad.
If she accepted the job offer, she wouldn't have moved abroad.
If she would have accepted the job offer, she wouldn't have moved abroad.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If she had accepted..., she wouldn't have moved...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: New employees are trained by senior staff.
New employees trains by senior staff.
New employees are training by senior staff.
New employees train by senior staff.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'are trained by senior staff.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The contract was signed yesterday afternoon.
The contract signed yesterday afternoon.
The contract was sign yesterday afternoon.
The contract is signed yesterday afternoon.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was signed yesterday afternoon.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The manager who hired me is retiring next month.
The manager which hired me is retiring next month.
The manager whom hired me is retiring next month.
The manager, who hired me, is retiring next month but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The manager who hired me...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My salary, which increased last year, still isn't enough.
My salary which increased last year still isn't enough but.
My salary, that increased last year, still isn't enough.
My salary which increased last year, still isn't enough.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'My salary, which increased last year, still isn't enough.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He must be new here, I've never seen him before.
He must to be new here, I've never seen him before.
He must being new here, I've never seen him before.
He musts be new here, I've never seen him before.
questions.explanation: 'Must' + base verb expresses a confident positive deduction: 'he must be new here.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The company could be planning layoffs.
The company could being planning layoffs.
The company could to be planning layoffs.
The company coulds be planning layoffs.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the company could be planning layoffs.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've sent ten job applications this month.
I've been sending ten job applications this month.
I've send ten job applications this month.
I'm sending ten job applications this month already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've sent ten job applications.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been saving money for a new car for a year.
I've saved money for a new car since a year.
I'm saving money for a new car for a year already.
I've been save money for a new car for a year.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been saving... for a year.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have finished the report.")
options: He said that he has finished the report.
He said that he had finished the report.
He said that he finished the report already.
He said he have finished the report.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'he had finished the report.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "When can you start?")
options: She asked me when can I start.
She asked me when I could start.
She asked me when could I start.
She asked me when I can start.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'she asked me when I could start.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to work night shifts before I changed careers.
I use to work night shifts before I changed careers.
I was used to work night shifts before I changed careers.
I used to working night shifts before I changed careers.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to work night shifts.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to managing a large budget now.
I'm used to manage a large budget now.
I use to managing a large budget now.
I'm used managing to a large budget now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to managing a large budget.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The company decided to take on more staff.
The company decided to take more staff on away.
The company decided to take on to more staff.
The company decided to take staff more on.
questions.explanation: 'Take on' means 'hire' or 'accept responsibility': 'take on more staff.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: They need to work out a new budget plan.
They need to work a new budget plan out to.
They need to work out to a new budget plan.
They need to work plan out a new budget.
questions.explanation: 'Work out' means 'calculate or solve': 'work out a new budget plan.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the low salary, she loves her job.
Despite of the low salary, she loves her job.
Although the low salary, she loves her job.
Despite the salary was low, she loves her job.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the low salary, she loves her job.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Sales dropped sharply. As a result, the store closed down.
Sales dropped sharply, as a result the store closed down.
As a result sales dropped sharply the store closed down.
Sales dropped sharply as a result, the store closed down.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'Sales dropped sharply. As a result, the store closed down.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough staff to finish the project on time.
We don't have staff enough to finish the project on time.
We don't have enough of staff to finish the project on time.
We hasn't enough staff to finish the project on time.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough staff.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is responsible for the whole finance team.
She is responsible of the whole finance team.
She is responsible to the whole finance team.
She is responsible on the whole finance team.
questions.explanation: 'Responsible for' + noun means 'in charge of': 'responsible for the finance team.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a company's HR department applying for a job?
options: Hey there,
Dear Hiring Manager,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Hiring Manager,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email applying for a job to a named contact?
options: Yours faithfully,
Kind regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Kind regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could send me the salary details.
I was wondering if you could to send me the salary details.
I was wondering could you sending me the salary details.
I wonder if you send could me the salary details.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could send me the details.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the entrepreneur.' and 'The entrepreneur's company grew fast.'?
options: This is the entrepreneur whose company grew fast.
This is the entrepreneur who company grew fast.
This is the entrepreneur which company grew fast.
This is the entrepreneur's company who grew fast.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the entrepreneur whose company grew fast.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never earned so much money before.
I have earned never so much money before.
Never I have earned so much money before.
I have earned so much money never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never earned so much money.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the contract has been approved.
I'd like to know whether has the contract been approved?
I'd like to know, whether the contract has been approved.
I'd like to know whether the contract has been approved?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time next month, I ___ at my new job.
options: will work
will be working
am working
work
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be working'.

questions.question: By the time I'm thirty, I ___ enough money for a house.
options: will save
will have saved
save
am saving
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have saved'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, update your CV. Secondly, prepare for interviews. Finally, negotiate your salary.
Firstly we update CV secondly prepare finally negotiate.
Finally update the CV, firstly prepare, secondly negotiate salary.
Secondly firstly update CV, finally prepare interviews.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't quit your job now, would you?
You wouldn't quit your job now, do you?
You wouldn't quit your job now, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't quit your job now, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't quit..., would you?'
